Same prompt, four models, four sharply different – and individually stable – distributions: GPT-4o spreads over 42/37/57, Claude Sonnet 5 concentrates on 47, Llama 3.3 on 53, and Qwen3-Max answers 42 every single time.

citing_sentences: Fig. 3 shows the verification ROC over 165 genuine and 27,060 impostor full-battery trials: $\mathrm{AUC}=0.971$, $\mathrm{EER}=7.3\%$.

citing_sentences: Fig. 4 and Table III quantify the operational trade-off by resampling random $k$-subsets of the 40 probe cells: a single cell already verifies far better than chance ($\mathrm{EER}=23.3\%$), eight cells reach $10.6\%$, and the curve flattens beyond $k\!\approx\!16$–24.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consumed through opaque serving chains – API aggregators, resellers, and inference providers – in which the client has no technical means to confirm that the model answering is the model advertised, and recent audits show that a substantial fraction of commercial endpoints deviate from the vendor’s reference weights. Existing identification techniques require long generated texts, token-level log-probabilities, adversarially crafted prompts, or the model owner’s cooperation. We show that far weaker evidence suffices. We define a behavioral fingerprint of an LLM as the empirical distribution of its answers to trivial one-word prompts – “name a random number between 1 and 100” – collected across four languages at a cost of one output token per query. Measuring 165 models served via a large commercial aggregator (OpenRouter), we find that (i) these distributions are highly non-uniform (median cell entropy 1.0 bit) and model-specific: split halves of the same model’s samples lie an order of magnitude closer than samples of different models; (ii) Jensen–Shannon divergence between fingerprints recovers model lineage, assigning a model to its documented family with 59.5% leave-one-out accuracy against an 18.4% chance rate; and (iii) a biometric-style verification protocol achieves a 7.3% equal error rate with the full 40-cell battery, and below 11% with eight probe cells – roughly a hundred single-token queries per audit. We further report ecosystem anomalies, including a proprietary-branded flagship endpoint distributionally indistinguishable from an open-weight Qwen model. The protocol, prompts, raw data, and analysis code are released for reproduction and operational use.

sections.body: The paper argues that clients of inference aggregators cannot confirm which model answers a request, and that providers may substitute cheaper or quantized models. It cites Gao et al. reporting that 11 of 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models were incompatible with reference weights. Existing identification methods need long outputs, engineered prompts, or full string samples. The proposed signal is the distribution of single-token answers to a trivial prompt such as naming a random number, which costs one answer token. The section poses four research questions on fingerprint existence, lineage recovery, verification, and ecosystem audit.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Served LLMs often differ from advertised models, so clients need a cheap, text-only identity check.

sections.body: The section places the work among attribution methods for generated images, speech, and text, and among API auditing studies. It notes that watermarks and backdoors need model-owner cooperation, so a third-party client cannot deploy them. It reports Sun et al. attributing full chat responses to source models with 97% five-way accuracy, but using long generations. It describes LLMmap, which identifies 42 model versions with eight engineered queries, and TRAP, which uses adversarial suffixes. The authors state their difference: they optimize what to measure, reading identity from answer distributions to fixed, innocuous prompts, and they claim no prior work uses single-token distributions at ecosystem scale.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior attribution work needs long outputs, logits, or owner cooperation; this study uses one-token answers.

sections.body: The threat model assumes a client who pays for a declared model X through an untrusted provider. The provider may serve X faithfully, serve a degraded variant, substitute a cheaper model Y, or route dynamically. The verifier can send ordinary chat requests and read text and standard metadata, and can query a trusted reference deployment. It has no logits or weights and a budget of at most a few hundred output tokens. Three adversary tiers are defined: oblivious substitution, filtering of known audit prompts, and emulation on arbitrary prompts. The protocol targets the first fully and the second by design through sampled paraphrase families. The third is said to reduce to faithfulness.
sections.heading: Threat Model
sections.headline: The verifier sees only text and a trusted reference, facing adversaries that substitute, filter, or emulate.

sections.body:
A fingerprint is the set of empirical answer distributions over a battery of probe cells, each a task crossed with a language. Ten tasks are used in English, Russian, Chinese, and Arabic, including random and favorite numbers, colors, animals, cities, and a coin flip. Each cell is sampled at temperature 1.0 with a one-word system prompt and a 16-token cap, and answers are normalized before counting. The distance between two models is the average Jensen–Shannon divergence in base 2 over cells with at least 10 valid samples:

$$
D(M_{a},M_{b})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}^{\prime}|}\sum_{(t,\ell)\in\mathcal{B}^{\prime}}\mathrm{JSD}\!\left(\hat{p}^{M_{a}}_{t,\ell}\,\|\,\hat{p}^{M_{b}}_{t,\ell}\right)
$$

Verification compares an endpoint with an enrolled reference using the mean divergence over the probe cells, and accepts the claim when the score is at most a threshold. Lineage uses average-linkage clustering and leave-one-out nearest-neighbour classification.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Each model is fingerprinted by answer distributions over ten tasks in four languages, compared with Jensen–Shannon divergence.

sections.body: The model list starts from a catalog snapshot of 342 models. Exclusions made by documented rules leave 165 models across 19 family labels and 53 serving providers. Exclusions cover non-text models, specialized models, rolling aliases, endpoints with mandatory hidden reasoning, and free-tier-only endpoints. Each model is sampled across 10 tasks and 4 languages, 30 times at temperature 1.0 and 3 times at temperature 0, with 15 repetitions for frontier-priced models. A pilot over 14 models fixed design choices before a pre-registered main run. The census totals 326,047 responses, with 23.3M input and 1.16M output tokens, costing USD 34.44, or USD 0.21 per model.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: The census covers 165 models from 342 catalog entries, 326,047 responses, and a total cost of USD 34.44.

sections.body: Single-token answers are strongly non-uniform, with a median cell entropy of 1.00 bit. Split halves of one model lie at a median divergence of 0.075, against 0.489 for different models. Across serving providers, the median cross-provider distance is 0.227, and verification against a reference from another provider still reaches AUC 0.880. Lineage recovery gives 59.5% leave-one-out accuracy against an 18.4% chance rate, with GLM and Mistral recovered well. Full-battery verification reaches AUC 0.971 and an equal error rate of 7.3%, which rises to 23.3% with one probe cell and 10.6% with eight. The ecosystem audit places writer/palmyra-x5 at distance 0.141 from a Qwen model, and ten of 34 same-model provider pairs diverge beyond the impostor range.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Fingerprints separate models and recover lineage at 59.5% accuracy against 18.4% chance, with 7.3% equal error rate verification.

sections.body: The discussion argues that single-token distributions reflect tokenizer segmentation, pre-training frequencies, post-training shifts, and decoding, so quantization and distillation perturb them. Replacing the serving provider moves a model's fingerprint by a median of 0.227, below the impostor median of 0.463. Against an adaptive provider, the battery uses semantic task classes rather than fixed magic strings, but a dedicated paraphrase-invariance experiment is left to future work. Caching is examined: 13.4% of census requests reported a prompt-cache hit, but a screen of 2,040 single-answer cells found no response-caching signature. The authors state that the protocol raises the cost of undetected substitution and gives no cryptographic guarantees.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Cross-provider shifts stay below impostor distances, and no response-caching signature appears in the census.

sections.body: The ethics section states that probing with ordinary chat requests within paid quotas raises no consent issues and involves no personal data. Anomalies are reported as statistical deviations, not accusations of fraud, because benign causes such as updated weights, sanctioned quantization, or caching layers can produce them. The authors say the findings are not security vulnerabilities, so coordinated disclosure norms do not apply, and they did not run a pre-publication notification process. Accountability is pursued through transparency: each finding is presented with its benign explanations, and raw data with timestamps and provider identifiers are released for independent checking. Dual-use aspects of shared-prior measurements are deferred to a companion study.
sections.heading: Ethics and Responsible Disclosure
sections.headline: Anomalies are framed as statistical deviations with benign explanations, and no security exploit is involved.

sections.body: The conclusion states that model identity leaks through the single token a model emits when asked a trivial question. It claims the distributions fingerprint models, reconstruct their genealogy, and support a verification protocol whose reliability-cost curve is quantified. It describes single-token auditing as a deployable, near-zero-cost forensic instrument as inference markets deepen. Listed future work includes longitudinal drift tracking, watermark-aware variants, and a companion analysis of tacit coordination between models.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Single-token audits are a near-zero-cost check, with longitudinal drift and watermark-aware variants left to future work.
